enrichment.short_title: R v Thomas: magic mushroom supply sentence appeal dismissed
key_facts: The appellant was found at Glastonbury with 73 self-sealing bags of dried magic mushrooms containing psilocybin, a Class A drug.
He admitted drying the mushrooms himself and told police they would sell for about £10 a bag; the PSR indicated some sales to cover his festival ticket.
The Crown Court imposed two years' imprisonment after trial for possession with intent to supply.
He appealed on grounds that custody was wrong in principle and that magic mushrooms should not be equated with other Class A drugs for sentencing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) appeal against sentence by leave of the Single Judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the two-year sentence was held proper for small-scale retail supply of a Class A drug.
enrichment.ratio: Courts should not distinguish between Class A drugs for sentencing purposes; supply of hallucinogenic drugs to facilitate use remains a very serious offence warranting substantial imprisonment, assessed by quantity rather than market value alone.
legal_issues: Whether the offence passed the custody threshold
Whether magic mushrooms should be treated differently from heroin or cocaine for sentencing
Whether dried self-picked mushrooms constitute a controlled preparation
Whether sufficient mitigation existed for good character and mental health difficulties

enrichment.short_title: Morecock v Parole Board: recall confirmed for driving offences on licence
key_facts: Morecock was released on licence after serving two-thirds of a twelve-year sentence for burglary with intent to rape and related violent and sexual offences.
The Secretary of State recalled him in May 2003 for breaching licence condition 5(vi) after contact with his ex-partner and unauthorised residence.
The Parole Board later confirmed recall principally because he drove without insurance and contrary to his provisional licence, offences that were not imprisonable.
He sought judicial review arguing the Board irrationally kept him in prison for minor road traffic offending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for judicial review of the Parole Board's rejection of representations against recall.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Parole Board's decision was held reasonably open and not irrational.
enrichment.ratio: Secretary of State directions on recall do not limit unacceptable risk of re-offending to serious or imprisonable offences; a prisoner remains in custody to serve the balance of the original determinate sentence and the Board may reject release on grounds different from those relied on at initial recall.
legal_issues: Whether unacceptable risk under the Secretary of State's directions is limited to serious or sexual re-offending
Whether recall for non-imprisonable driving offences is oppressive
Whether inconsistent reasoning between the Secretary of State and Parole Board renders the decision unlawful
Whether the claimant was unlikely to comply with licence conditions in future

enrichment.short_title: Gaoua v SSHD: Algerian asylum and Article 3 case remitted to IAT
key_facts: An Algerian Berber was arrested in Leicester in January 2002 with others in anti-terrorism raids linked to Benmerzouga and Meziane.
He was not charged under terrorism legislation but convicted of passport and employment fraud; he claimed asylum fearing detention and torture on return to Algeria.
An adjudicator allowed his appeal but the Immigration Appeal Tribunal reversed; the Secretary of State conceded the IAT decision was flawed.
The Court of Appeal had to decide whether to reinstate the adjudicator's decision or remit for rehearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision refusing asylum and human rights protection.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; both the Refugee Convention and Article 3 issues remitted to a differently constituted Immigration Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: Where the adjudicator may have elided asylum and Article 3 grounds and failed to identify the persecutor's real reason for mistreatment, and where IAT reasoning conflicted with a similar case, remittal to a fresh tribunal is the proper remedy rather than reinstatement.
legal_issues: Whether to reinstate the adjudicator's decision or remit to the IAT
Whether persecution for suspected terrorist association amounts to persecution for political opinion
Whether the adjudicator properly separated Convention and Article 3 analysis
Whether expert reports on Algerian country conditions were adequately considered

enrichment.short_title: Johnson v MDU: CPR disclosure after failed Data Protection access request
key_facts: Consultant surgeon David Johnson sued the Medical Defence Union after it refused to renew his membership under Article 11(a).
He claimed improper processing of personal data and sought section 7 access, section 10 blocking, section 13 damages and section 14 rectification.
A preliminary issue held the MDU had complied with his section 7 request because disputed documents were not personal data under Durant.
He then applied for wide CPR specific disclosure of the same material for his substantive DPA claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court interim application on specific disclosure and Part 18 requests in ongoing DPA proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: In principle a failed section 7(9) application does not prevent CPR disclosure for sections 10, 13 and 14 claims; the court directed answers to three Part 18 requests but deferred any disclosure order until pleadings were amended.
enrichment.ratio: Section 15(2) restricts disclosure only in section 7(9) access proceedings and does not fetter CPR disclosure in separate claims for breach of data protection principles; manual files not in a relevant filing system may be disclosable in such claims though outside section 7.
legal_issues: Whether CPR disclosure can circumvent section 7 and section 15(2) DPA restrictions
Whether documents withheld on a section 7 application remain immune from disclosure in sections 10, 13 and 14 proceedings
Whether third-party confidentiality concerns under the DPA affect CPR disclosure discretion
Which Part 18 requests should be answered at this stage

enrichment.short_title: Holmes v Portugal: extradition refused for unexplained delay and prejudice
key_facts: Holmes and his wife were accused of passing counterfeit £20 notes at an Albufeira bureau de change in September 1998.
They were bailed in Portugal in September 1998 but returned to England; trial was adjourned in February 2000 when they had not been served.
No service was attempted within the 20 days ordered; an international arrest warrant followed years later and he was arrested in February 2004.
He applied for habeas corpus arguing the delay made return unjust or oppressive and prejudiced his defence witnesses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court habeas corpus application following committal for extradition to Portugal.
enrichment.outcome: Applicant discharged; return to Portugal held oppressive because of unexplained delay, false sense of security and prejudice to defence witnesses.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 11(3)(b) of the 1989 Act, wholly unexplained delay after an order for expedition, combined with loss of key witnesses and a defendant's reasonable belief proceedings had ended, can make extradition oppressive even for non-trivial counterfeiting offences.
legal_issues: Whether the counterfeiting charges were trivial under section 11(3)(a)
Whether passage of time since 1998 made return unjust or oppressive under section 11(3)(b)
Whether delay prejudiced the ability to obtain defence evidence from the ex-wife and others
Whether bail conditions in Portugal bound the applicant to remain for trial

enrichment.short_title: O2 v Hutchison 3G: interim relief refused on mobile price comparison ad
key_facts: O2 sought interim injunctions restraining Hutchison 3G television, press and radio ads comparing pay-as-you-go call prices.
The TV ad opened with O2-branded bubbles and compared a first three-minute peak call at 75p with ThreePay at 15p based on a £25 voucher.
O2 complained the comparison was misleading and that use of bubbles and O2 marks infringed registered trade marks.
3 argued the comparison was fair and protected as honest comparative advertising under section 10(6) and Article 12(b).
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court interim injunction application in trade mark infringement and comparative advertising dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Interim relief refused; the price comparison was held at least strongly arguable as fair and honest, with only an arguable bubbles mark infringement case.
enrichment.ratio: Community and domestic law permit honest comparative advertising using a competitor's mark where indispensable; a literally simplified price comparison is not significantly misleading if its headline message is true for the target market spending at least £15 per month, and Jacob J's criteria govern honest practices at interlocutory stage.
legal_issues: Whether the ThreePay price comparison was misleading or dishonest
Whether use of O2 marks and bubble imagery infringed registered trade marks
Whether section 10(6) and Article 12(b) protect the comparative use
Whether lost voucher minutes rendered the advertised rate materially misleading

enrichment.short_title: R v EW: historic sexual abuse convictions upheld, sentence reduced

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: The appellant was convicted of buggery and indecent assaults against his step-grandson M and indecent assault against stepdaughter S dating from the 1970s.
Alleged offences spanned 1971 to 1980; Marianne, the central household witness, had died in 1999 before trial.
The Recorder refused abuse of process stays and left counts to the jury, who acquitted on two counts relating to S.
He was sentenced to eight years total; the Court of Appeal upheld convictions but reduced the total to six years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeals against conviction and sentence in historic intra-familial sexual abuse prosecution.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal partly allowed with total sentence reduced from eight to six years.
enrichment.ratio: Delay alone does not require a stay where a fair trial remains possible with proper jury directions; the residual B discretion to quash is exceptional and not warranted here, but totality required reduction given age, health and the narrow basis of conviction on count 2.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings should have been stayed as an abuse of process for delay
Whether there was no case to answer on counts relating to S
Whether summing-up on the Elliott Hotel incident date was adequate
Whether the eight-year total sentence was manifestly excessive

enrichment.short_title: Eco-Energy v SSHD: no person aggrieved status for planning appeal company
key_facts: Eco-Energy Group applied for planning permission for coal extraction land and lost at public inquiry; decision issued 22 December 2003.
On 24 January 2004 Mr Clarke orally purported to assign his land option to EE Ltd, which filed a section 288 challenge on the last day.
Collins J struck out the claim because EE Ltd was not a person aggrieved; on appeal it sought to rely on equitable estoppel and assignment of the planning application.
Mr Clarke was the sole shareholder of EE Ltd and could not substitute as claimant without being out of time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against strike-out of a section 288 planning challenge for lack of standing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs; EE Ltd could not establish person aggrieved status and could not substitute Mr Clarke under CPR 19.5.
enrichment.ratio: A person aggrieved under section 288 requires a relevant land interest or active participation in the inquiry; an ineffective oral option assignment and a new equitable estoppel case cannot confer standing, nor can assignment of a determined planning application transfer the exclusive right to appeal held by the original applicant.
legal_issues: Who qualifies as a person aggrieved under section 288
Whether an oral option assignment creates standing despite section 2 of the 1989 Act
Whether equitable estoppel can arise between a sole shareholder and his company
Whether CPR 19.5 permits substituting Mr Clarke after the section 288 time limit

enrichment.short_title: Kilcarne v Targetfollow: Baskerville House joint venture and equity claim fails
key_facts: Kilcarne lent about £7.5 million secured on charges over Baskerville House, Birmingham, to fund Targetfollow's leasehold development.
Mr Naghshineh of Targetfollow and Mr Singh of Kilcarne discussed a possible joint venture and profit-sharing if the development were sold before January 2007.
Kilcarne claimed an enforceable joint venture agreement, equitable interest and quantum meruit for monitoring services by Mr Singh.
Targetfollow completed much of the development using Kilcarne's funding but disputes arose over repayment and control.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial on liability in a complex property development and secured lending dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Kilcarne's registered caution against Baskerville House must be vacated.
enrichment.ratio: February 2002 discussions did not create an enforceable joint venture contract; Kilcarne had no expectation of such an agreement and incurred monitoring costs in reliance on its security and possible profit share on sale, not on a contract that failed to materialise.
legal_issues: Whether February 2002 dealings created a binding joint venture agreement
Whether equitable interest arose in Kilcarne's favour and how it should be satisfied
Whether Targetfollow owed a duty to progress development with due dispatch
Whether Kilcarne was entitled to quantum meruit for Mr Singh's monitoring services

enrichment.short_title: Tombs v Wilson Connolly: bricklaying sub-contractor liable for defects
key_facts: Mr Tombs, a bricklaying sub-contractor, claimed unpaid work of £48,047 and £101,604 for wrongful repudiation after leaving Wilson Connolly sites in April 2003.
WCL counterclaimed for defective work including rebuilding at 2 Comfrey Way, missing wall ties at Pine Lea and snagging items.
The judge found Tombs wrongfully repudiated by withdrawing labour over a non-payment that did not amount to repudiatory breach.
Outstanding work valued at £26,847.90 was offset by defect damages of £25,092.62 and £56,112.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of sub-contract payment, repudiation and defects claims.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for WCL in the sum of £54,356.72 after set-off of claim and counterclaim.
enrichment.ratio: Withdrawal of labour over one unpaid interim application without justification constituted wrongful repudiation by the sub-contractor; failure to pay a single instalment is not ordinarily repudiatory, and defect recovery must be limited to natural and direct remedial costs.
legal_issues: Whether WCL or Mr Tombs repudiated the sub-contracts in April 2003
Whether non-payment of 27/28 March 2003 applications was repudiatory
Whether Tombs could recover loss of profit on unstarted plots
What remedial costs were recoverable for wall tie and Bull property defects
